info.name: MAW Foundation — Sample Server
info.description:
Dynamic RBAC sample-server (`createDynamicExpressAuth` + module registry) plus the auth foundation from `@maw/auth-core`.

**Setup**
1. `npm run sample:server`
2. Import this collection + `local.postman_environment.json`
3. Select **MAW Foundation — Local**
4. Run **Login as Owner** (or Manager / Clerk) — tests persist `accessToken` / `refreshToken` / `sessionId` on the **collection**

Protected routes send `Authorization: Bearer {{accessToken}}`.

Permission codes are `Action_Module` (e.g. `Read_Reports`). Owner is a superuser and bypasses checks. Manager/clerk use the seeded role map.

**Folder order matters.** Folders 1–4 are written to run top-to-bottom in the Collection Runner: authentication seeds the tokens, the account lifecycle folder registers a throwaway user and carries its tokens forward, and the MFA folder enrolls and then disables MFA so the run is repeatable.

**Login rate limit.** `/auth/login` allows 5 requests per minute per IP (`DEFAULT_SECURITY_CONFIG.rateLimit.login`), and the collection logs in about a dozen times, so a back-to-back full pass will hit `429`. Every login tolerates that and reports a skip instead of a failure, and anything that would act on the wrong account is skipped with it. Run one folder at a time, or space the requests out:

```
newman run MAW-Foundation.postman_collection.json --env-var baseUrl=http://localhost:4000 --delay-request 13000
```

**One-time tokens.** The sample has no mail provider, so email-verification and password-reset tokens are written to the **server log** rather than returned by the API. Copy the token from the console into `verificationToken` / `resetToken` before running those requests.

**Seeded users** (password `password123`)
| Email | Role | Audience | `/reports` | `/orders` | `/inventory` | `GET /billing` | `POST /billing` | `GET /audit-logs` | `GET /audit-logs/export` | `/admin/users` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| owner@demo.test | owner | admin | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 | 200 |
| manager@demo.test | manager | admin | 200 | 200 | 200 | 403 (no `Read_Billing`) | 200 | 200 | 403 (no `Export_AuditLogs`) | 403 (no `Read_Users`) |
| clerk@demo.test | clerk | operator | 403 | 200 | 403 | 403 (no `Read_Billing`) | 200 | 403 (wrong audience) | 403 (wrong audience) | 403 (wrong audience) |

request.description:
`AuthenticationService` returns the same `Invalid credentials` body for a wrong password and for an unknown email, and spends the same time on both (it verifies against a decoy hash when no user matches), so neither the response nor the latency reveals which emails are registered.

After 5 consecutive failures the key is locked out and even the correct password returns `423 ACCOUNT_LOCKED`.

item.name: 2. Account lifecycle
item.description:
Registration → email verification → password change → forgot/reset, served by `RegistrationService`, `EmailVerification`, `PasswordChangeService` and `PasswordResetService`.

**Run this folder in order.** `POST Register` mints a unique throwaway email into `{{newUserEmail}}` and the later requests reuse it, so the folder is repeatable without cleaning the database.

**Manual step.** Verification and reset tokens are logged by the server, not returned by the API (no mail provider is configured in the sample). Copy the `token: '…'` value from the server console into the `verificationToken` / `resetToken` collection variables before running those two requests.

exec: // Unique address per run so re-running the folder never hits DUPLICATE_EMAIL.
console.log('Registered', pm.collectionVariables.get('newUserEmail'), '— copy the verification token from the server log into {{verificationToken}}');

request.description: Creates the user with `accountStatus: PENDING_VERIFICATION` (`registration.requireEmailVerification` is on) and issues a verification token. The response deliberately omits the token — it goes to the configured mail transport, which in this sample is the server log.
`validatePassword` runs before the user is created, so nothing is persisted. `violations` lists every rule that failed rather than only the first.

**Set `{{resetToken}}` first** from the server log line `Password reset token issued`.

On success every server-side session for that user is revoked (`PasswordResetService` calls `sessionService.revokeAll`), which is what logs a thief out of stolen devices. Single-use and expiring, like the verification token.

item.name: 3. Sessions & devices
item.description:
Server-side sessions from `SessionService`. Every login writes one row carrying device, IP and user agent, which is what powers a "where you're signed in" screen and remote sign-out.

Self-contained: the first request signs in so the folder can be run on its own, and the rest act on the `{{sessionId}}` it captures.

exec: pm.test.skip('login rate-limited (5/min) — wait a minute and re-run');

request.description: Creates the session the rest of this folder inspects and revokes. The device headers are what appear as `deviceInfo` in the listing — change them and log in again to see a second device.

exec: pm.test('includes the session this token came from', function () {

request.description:
Only live sessions are returned — revoked and expired rows are filtered out. Log in from another client (or change `x-device-id`) to watch the list grow.

The seeded config allows 5 concurrent sessions; a sixth login silently revokes the oldest.

Revokes one session by id — the "sign this device out" action. Re-run **GET Sessions** and it is gone.

The matching access JWT keeps working until it expires, because it is stateless; the session row governs refresh and the device list.

query.description: Session to keep alive — normally the caller's own, so "sign out everywhere else" does not sign you out here. Drop it to revoke every session.

request.description: "Sign out everywhere else". The same call `PasswordResetService` makes after a reset, except that one keeps nothing.

item.name: 4. MFA
item.description:
TOTP second factor via `MfaService` — enroll, activate, then a two-leg login.

`{{mfaCode}}` is computed for you: the collection pre-request script derives a live RFC 6238 code from `{{mfaSecret}}` before every request, so these can be sent without an authenticator app.

**Run in order.** The folder is self-contained: it signs in as `{{mfaEmail}}` (the seeded `clerk@demo.test`), enrolls, exercises both the TOTP and backup-code paths, then disables MFA again — so it leaves the account exactly as it found it and can be re-run.

exec: // Enrollment follows the bearer token, so the rest of the folder only
// runs once we know the token belongs to the intended MFA subject.
pm.test.skip('login rate-limited (5/min) — wait a minute and re-run');
pm.test('signed in as the MFA test user', function () {

request.description: Enrollment acts on whoever the bearer token belongs to, so the folder starts by signing in as its own subject. Point `{{mfaEmail}}` at a different account to enroll that one instead.

exec: console.log('Skipped — run POST Login (MFA test user) first so this enrolls the intended account.');

request.description:
Generates the TOTP secret plus 10 backup codes. This is the only time either is returned in the clear: the secret is stored encrypted (`MFA_ENCRYPTION_KEY`) and the backup codes are stored as salted hashes.

Enrolling does **not** turn MFA on — **POST Activate MFA** does, after proving the authenticator works. `otpauthUri` is what you render as a QR code.

exec: console.log('Skipped — run POST Enroll MFA first.');

request.description: Confirms the enrolled secret by checking one live code, then sets `mfaEnabled` on the user. From here every login for this account needs a second factor.

First leg. Credentials are correct, so instead of tokens you get a short-lived (5 min) challenge token and no session is created yet.

The challenge is stored as a hash and carries the `rememberMe` flag forward, so the password never has to be re-sent for the second leg.

item.name: 5. User
item.description: `GET /me` returns the current user plus their `permissions` list (UI permission payload). `GET /admin/users` is the admin user list, gated by `Read_Users` + admin audience.

request.description: Requires Bearer token. Payload: `{ userId, tenantId, role, audience, permissions }`. Use `permissions` for UI gates (`Action_Module` codes).

`requireAuth` + `audienceGuard('admin')` + `requirePermission('Read_Users')`.

- Owner → 200 (superuser bypass)
- Manager → 403 `{ error, permission: "Read_Users", reason }`
- Clerk → 403 `{ error: "wrong audience", expected: "admin" }`

item.name: 7. Teardown
item.description: Runs last so the folders above still have a token. Logging out mid-collection would strand every request after it.

request.description: Revokes the refresh token, and the server-side session too when `sessionId` is supplied — that is what drops the device out of `GET /auth/sessions`. The access JWT stays valid until it expires, since it is stateless; this script clears the local collection tokens.
